newsitem.title: PERU: Navy combs Boeing crash site in Peruvian Pacific.
newsitem.headline: Navy combs Boeing crash site in Peruvian Pacific.

text.p: The Peruvian navy on Thursday combed the site of a plane crash off Peru's Pacific coast where all 70 aboard a Boeing 757-200 belonging to local airline Aeroperu were killed early on Wednedsay.
Navy captain Augusto Zegarra told Reuters only 10 bodies and floating scraps of wreckage had been recovered from the sea by early Thursday despite an all-night rescue operation.

"The problem is that the central part of the fuselage is too deep, at around 150 yards (150 meters) below the surface," he said, adding that most of the bodies were almost certainly still trapped in the wreckage.

Two helicopters, two navy frigates and private boats were leading a search that began before dawn on Wednesday after the Boeing suffered technical problems en route to Chile and plunged into the ocean.
Relatives of the victims, who came from 11 countries, were arriving on Thursday at Lima along with an investigative team.

Officials of Boeing Co., engine maker Pratt & Whitney, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transporation Safety Board, reportedly arrived in Lima from the United States on Thursday and were set to head to the crash site to assist Peruvian investigators.
However, Boeing officials in Lima declined to comment on the investigative team or the cause of the crash.
Peruvian Transport Minister Elsa Carrera de Escalante has blamed computer problems on the plane for the accident while Aeroperu cited "technical failures" without elaborating.

The final words of pilot, Eric Schreiber, to Lima air traffic control were: "I am reducing engine power, but the plane is still accelerating," according to a transcript of the message quoted by Carrera.
President Alberto Fujimori said the jet was new with only three months of flying. It had all the necessary guarantees and was flown by an experienced pilot.
Meanwhile, opposition legislators called on Carrera to answer questions in Congress about Peru's recent history of plane accidents.

Wednesday's crash, one of the worst in Peru's aviation history, came seven months after a Boeing 737 belonging to local Faucett airline crashed and killed all 123 people on board near Peru's second city, Arequipa.
Since 1967, a total of 601 people have been killed in air crashes in Peru.
Aeroperu, privatised in 1993 and owned by Aeromexico, said it was operating flights normally Thursday.

The crash was the third involving a 757, which had a perfect safety record from the time it entered commercial service in 1983 until last year, when an American Airlines jet slammed into a mountain in Colombia, killing 159 people.
In February, a 757-200 crashed into the Caribbean shortly after taking off from the Dominican Republic, killing all 189 people aboard. Both crashes were blamed on pilot error.
